# /feature: POST /inventory/{skuId} — receive stock for a SKU

Follow these steps in order. Do not skip one because the feature looks small.

**Robert writes the production code; you coach.** Never create or edit files under `src/main/`
unless Robert explicitly asks for that specific edit (see "Who writes what" in `CLAUDE.md`).
Your deliverables are the contract check, the plan, the tests, hints, reviews and the docs.

## 0. Gate: previous walkthrough done?

Check the newest file in `docs/learning/walkthroughs/`. If there are commits touching
`src/` after the commit it records, a walkthrough is still owed. Tell Robert and suggest
running `/walkthrough` first. Continue only if he says to.

## 1. Pin the behavior to the contract

Read `src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml` and quote the exact part this feature implements.
List the acceptance criteria as a checklist: method + path, request schema and validation,
every response status with its content type (`application/json` vs `text/plain`), and body shape.
List any ambiguity the contract leaves open and ask Robert how to resolve it.

## 2. Plan, then wait for approval

Give a short plan covering:

- the files Robert will create or change, each one's layer (controller / service / repository /
  model / migration), and what each needs to do, described in words and signatures, not code;
- the test files you will write, and which acceptance criterion each test covers;
- the Kotlin and Spring concepts this feature introduces for the first time. That list is both
  what you'll coach him through and the agenda for the walkthrough.

**Stop and wait for Robert to approve the plan.**

## 3. Write the failing tests

- Write the tests under `src/test/` first: at least one per acceptance criterion, covering the
  error paths as well as the happy path. They are the spec for Robert's code.
- Tests reference the classes and functions named in the plan. The build won't compile until he
  creates them; that's expected. Tell him which compile errors and failures to expect.
- Follow the documentation standard in `CLAUDE.md` for the test files (KDoc, `// Why:`, notes
  header line).

## 4. Robert writes the code; you coach

- Create the marker file `.claude/coding-in-progress` (gitignored). While it exists, the
  `check_notes` Stop hook skips `src/main/`, so it won't push you to document half-finished code.
- Hand over a short checklist: which file to write next and what it must do, in request-path
  order (usually migration → model → repository → service → controller). Suggest a first
  test to make pass.
- **Hints go in increasing order**: the concept → the API or annotation to look up → the shape
  of the code in words → a code snippet, but only when he asks, and in chat for him to type.
  Never write the file for him.
- Explain concepts when he asks or when you see him stuck on one, with the Java equivalent
  when that helps.
- Run the build (`.\gradlew.bat build` in PowerShell) when he asks, and explain failures in terms of what his
  code does. Report results truthfully.
- The KDoc hook only runs on your edits, so remind him that every non-private declaration he
  writes needs KDoc, plus the `// Study notes:` header line.
- While his code is in progress, its study notes are expected to lag. Don't write notes for
  half-finished code.
- If you ever try to edit `src/main/`, the `code_guard` hook asks Robert for approval. Don't
  request that unless he asked for that specific edit.

## 4b. Review

When the tests pass, review his code: contract conformance, idiomatic Kotlin (flag
Java-style Kotlin and explain the idiom), the documentation standard, and anything the tests
don't catch. Explain each point; he makes the changes. Rerun the build after his fixes.

## 5. Documentation

Once the build is green and the review is done, run `/sync-docs`. It writes or updates the
study notes for every changed file (describing the code Robert wrote), the concepts
index, the README (endpoint status, curl examples, decision records) and the TODO, then runs
the `doc-reviewer` agent until it returns `PASS`. Tell Robert what the reviewer caught.

## 6. Check the docs gate

`python scripts/check_notes.py` must print nothing. (The Stop hook enforces this too.)

## 7. Hand-off

Summarize what Robert built and what he learned along the way. Propose a commit message (small and descriptive, ending with the
attribution line from the system reminder), and commit only if Robert says so. Finish with:
"Ready for `/walkthrough`, then `/ship`." Do not start another feature in this turn.

openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: Inventory API
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /inventory/{skuId}:
    parameters:
      - name: skuId
        in: path
        required: true
        schema:
          type: string
          example: CW-XYCS-BM-01
    get:
      summary: Get inventory for a SKU
      description: Returns the current quantity on hand for the specified SKU. Returns 404 if the SKU does not exist.
      operationId: getInventory
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Current inventory state for the sku
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/InventoryItem'
        '404':
          description: SKU not found
          content:
            text/plain:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Error'
    post:
      summary: Create or update inventory for a SKU
      description: >
        Adds stock for the specified SKU. If the SKU does not yet exist in inventory,
        it is created with the given quantity. If it already exists, the quantity is
        added to the current stock. Returns the updated inventory state for the SKU.
      operationId: createInventory
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/InventoryQuantity'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Current state of the item after update
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/InventoryItem'
        '400':
          description: Invalid request
          content:
            text/plain:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Error'
  /inventory/{skuId}/purchase:
    parameters:
      - name: skuId
        in: path
        required: true
        schema:
          type: string
          example: widget
    post:
      summary: Purchase a quantity of a SKU
      description: >
        Deducts the requested quantity from inventory for the specified SKU.
        The purchase is only allowed if the current stock is sufficient to
        fulfill the full requested quantity. Returns 404 if the SKU does not
        exist. Returns 400 if there is insufficient inventory. On success, returns the
        remaining inventory for the SKU.
      operationId: purchaseItem
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/InventoryQuantity'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Purchase successful; remaining inventory for the item
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/InventoryItem'
        '400':
          description: Insufficient inventory or invalid request
          content:
            text/plain:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Error'
        '404':
          description: SKU not found
          content:
            text/plain:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Error'
  /inventory:
    get:
      summary: List all inventory
      description: >
        Returns a list of all SKUs currently in inventory along with their quantities.
        If no SKUs exist, returns an empty array.
      operationId: listInventory
      responses:
        '200':
          description: List of all inventory items
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: array
                items:
                  $ref: '#/components/schemas/InventoryItem'  
components:
  schemas:
    InventoryQuantity:
      type: object
      required:
        - quantity
      properties:
        quantity:
          type: integer
          minimum: 1
          example: 10
    InventoryItem:
      type: object
      properties:
        skuId:
          type: string
          example: widget
        quantity:
          type: integer
          minimum: 0
          example: 10
    Error:
      type: string
      example: Insufficient inventory# TODO

## Oversell protection: test plan

**Invariant: a purchase must never oversell, even when requests arrive at the same moment.**
Stock never goes below zero, and every unit sold was actually in stock. Test this at every
level we build, using several different mechanisms, because each one catches a different
class of bug. Each item below is also a teaching topic for a walkthrough.

### Correctness in isolation
- [ ] Repository tests against a real Postgres (Testcontainers, not H2): purchase exact stock → 0,
      purchase stock + 1 → rejected and quantity unchanged, purchase on missing SKU → not found
- [ ] Controller tests (`MockMvc`): 400 with `text/plain` body on insufficient stock, 404 on missing SKU

### Concurrency
- [ ] **Same-SKU purchase race.** Seed stock S, fire N > S concurrent purchases of 1 through
      a start gate (`CountDownLatch` or coroutines) so they really overlap. Assert: exactly S
      succeed (200), N − S are rejected (400), final quantity is 0, never negative.
- [ ] **Uneven quantities.** Concurrent purchases of different sizes. Assert: the sum of
      successful purchases ≤ S, and final = S − sum(successful).
- [ ] **Mixed receive + purchase race.** Concurrent restocks and purchases. Assert:
      final = initial + sum(received) − sum(successful purchases).
- [ ] **New-SKU creation race.** Concurrent first-time `POST`s for a SKU that doesn't exist yet.
      All succeed, no duplicate-key errors, final = sum of all quantities.
- [ ] **Repeat to flush out flakiness.** Run the race tests many times (`@RepeatedTest`), since
      concurrency bugs are intermittent.
- [ ] **Negative control.** Temporarily swap in a naive read-then-write implementation and show
      the race test *fails*. This proves the test can actually detect an oversell.

### Database backstop
- [ ] Test that the `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint rejects a direct update that would go
      negative, so the database protects the data even if the application has a bug.
      (test written in `InventoryRepositoryTest` 2026-09-24; passes once Robert's V1 migration exists)

### Across instances and under load
- [ ] **Multiple app instances.** Two app instances (or two Spring contexts) against the same
      Postgres, running the purchase race. Correctness must hold because the database enforces it.
- [ ] **HTTP load test.** Gatling (it has a Kotlin DSL) or k6 against the running app: sustained
      concurrent purchases on hot SKUs, then check the final quantities with `GET /inventory`.

## Oversell protection: test plan

**Invariant: a purchase must never oversell, even when requests arrive at the same moment.**
Stock never goes below zero, and every unit sold was actually in stock. Test this at every
level we build, using several different mechanisms, because each one catches a different
class of bug. Each item below is also a teaching topic for a walkthrough.

### Correctness in isolation
- [ ] Repository tests against a real Postgres (Testcontainers, not H2): purchase exact stock → 0,
      purchase stock + 1 → rejected and quantity unchanged, purchase on missing SKU → not found
- [ ] Controller tests (`MockMvc`): 400 with `text/plain` body on insufficient stock, 404 on missing SKU

### Concurrency
- [ ] **Same-SKU purchase race.** Seed stock S, fire N > S concurrent purchases of 1 through
      a start gate (`CountDownLatch` or coroutines) so they really overlap. Assert: exactly S
      succeed (200), N − S are rejected (400), final quantity is 0, never negative.
- [ ] **Uneven quantities.** Concurrent purchases of different sizes. Assert: the sum of
      successful purchases ≤ S, and final = S − sum(successful).
- [ ] **Mixed receive + purchase race.** Concurrent restocks and purchases. Assert:
      final = initial + sum(received) − sum(successful purchases).
- [ ] **New-SKU creation race.** Concurrent first-time `POST`s for a SKU that doesn't exist yet.
      All succeed, no duplicate-key errors, final = sum of all quantities.
- [ ] **Repeat to flush out flakiness.** Run the race tests many times (`@RepeatedTest`), since
      concurrency bugs are intermittent.
- [ ] **Negative control.** Temporarily swap in a naive read-then-write implementation and show
      the race test *fails*. This proves the test can actually detect an oversell.

## Step 2: Plan

The decision records (all four go in the README): exact-match SKUs, strict JSON, overflow returns 400, wrong Content-Type returns 400.

### What you'll write (request-path order)

| # | File | Layer | What it does |
|---|------|-------|--------------|
| 1 | `build.gradle.kts` | build | Add `spring-boot-starter-validation`, for Bean Validation. |
| 2 | `application.yml` | config | Make Jackson strict: no float→int truncation and no `"5"`→`5` coercion. |
| 3 | `inventory/InventoryQuantity.kt` *(new)* | model | Request body: `data class InventoryQuantity(val quantity: Int)`, named after the contract schema, with a `@Min(1)` constraint. |
| 4 | `InventoryRepository.kt` | repository | `fun addStock(skuId: String, quantity: Int): InventoryItem?` does one atomic upsert: `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (sku_id) DO UPDATE SET quantity = inventory.quantity + EXCLUDED.quantity WHERE <no overflow> RETURNING sku_id, quantity`. It returns the new row, or `null` when the add would overflow. |
| 5 | `error/<your name>Exception.kt` *(new)* | error | Thrown when adding stock would overflow. You pick the name. |
| 6 | `InventoryService.kt` | service | `fun receiveInventory(skuId: String, quantity: Int): InventoryItem` calls `addStock` and throws the overflow exception on `null` (same `?: throw` shape you used in `getInventory`). |
| 7 | `InventoryController.kt` | controller | `@PostMapping("/{skuId}")` taking `@PathVariable skuId` and `@Valid @RequestBody body: InventoryQuantity`. |
| 8 | `InventoryExceptionHandler.kt` | error | Four new handlers, all 400 `text/plain`: validation failure, unreadable body, unsupported media type, and your overflow exception. |

Why the overflow guard sits in the SQL `WHERE`: this is the same pattern purchase will use (`UPDATE ... WHERE quantity >= ?`). The database decides atomically, and "no row came back" means "rejected". There's also a nice detail inside the check: `a + b <= MAX` would itself overflow, so you rewrite it as `a <= MAX - b`.

### 400 message text (exact strings the tests will check)

- `quantity` < 1: `quantity must be at least 1`
- Unreadable body (malformed JSON, empty body, `{}`, `null`, `"5"`, `1.5`, `3000000000`): `Invalid request body`
- Wrong Content-Type: `Content-Type must be application/json`
- Overflow: `Quantity would exceed the maximum stock`

### Tests I'll write

- **`InventoryRepositoryTest`** (+7): creates a new SKU; adds to an existing SKU; adds to a zero-stock SKU; leaves other SKUs untouched (a decoy row); reaches exactly `Int.MAX_VALUE`; returns `null` with stock unchanged on overflow; creates a separate row for a different-case SKU.
- **`InventoryControllerTest`** (+~8): new SKU → 200 JSON; existing → summed total; `0` and `-5` → 400 with stock unchanged; one parameterized test over every unreadable body → 400 `Invalid request body`; wrong Content-Type → 400; overflow → 400 with stock unchanged; case-sensitive SKU.
- **`InventoryConcurrencyTest`** *(new, from the oversell plan)*: 50 threads race a first-time `addStock` on the same SKU behind a `CountDownLatch` start gate, and 50 threads race an add to an existing SKU. Both assert no exceptions and final = sum. `@RepeatedTest(5)`. This one can't be `@JdbcTest`: its per-test rollback transaction would hide the rows from the other threads.

### New concepts (coaching list + walkthrough agenda)

- **Kotlin:** annotation use-site targets (`@field:Min`), and how the project's `-Xannotation-default-target=param-property` flag affects them; plus request DTOs as data classes.
- **Spring:** `@PostMapping`, `@RequestBody`, Bean Validation with `@Valid`, and the three framework exceptions (`MethodArgumentNotValidException`, `HttpMessageNotReadableException`, `HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException`) and how the advice turns them into responses.
- **Jackson 3:** coercion and strictness settings through `application.yml`.
- **SQL:** Postgres upsert (`ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE`, `EXCLUDED`, a conditional `WHERE`, `RETURNING`), why one statement is race-free, and how to write an overflow check that can't overflow itself.
- **Testing:** start gates, thread pools and `@RepeatedTest` for concurrency tests.

One choice for you: the plan puts the `quantity >= 1` check in the **controller layer via Bean Validation**. That's idiomatic Spring and it teaches use-site targets. The alternative is a manual check in the service that throws your own exception. It's simpler, and it also protects callers that skip the controller, but it's less idiomatic.

"""Stop hook: every source file must have study notes that are at least as new as the code.

The code carries only short KDoc and one-line `// Why:` / `// Contract:` comments. The teaching
lives in docs/learning/notes/, one Markdown file per source file (see the README there for the
mapping). This hook keeps the two from drifting apart.

Claude Code runs it when Claude is about to end its turn (see .claude/settings.json). For each
source file it compares "when did this last change" for the file and for its notes:

  - a file with uncommitted changes (modified, staged or untracked): its modification time
  - a committed, unchanged file: the time of the last commit that touched it

If the code is newer than its notes, or the notes are missing, the script prints what's stale to
stderr and exits 2. Claude Code then keeps Claude working with that message as feedback, and
Claude runs /sync-docs. It also reports notes whose source file no longer exists.

To avoid an endless loop, it never blocks twice in a row: when Claude Code says a Stop hook
already sent Claude back to work (`stop_hook_active`), the script lets the turn end.

While Robert is writing production code (the marker file .claude/coding-in-progress exists,
created by /feature and removed by /sync-docs), files under src/main/ and their notes are

# InventoryControllerTest.kt

> Source: [src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryControllerTest.kt](../../../../../src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryControllerTest.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-27

## Role

Tests `GET /inventory` and `GET /inventory/{skuId}` through the whole stack: MockMvc →
controller → service → repository → real Postgres. It checks exactly what the contract
specifies: the status code, the `Content-Type` and the exact body (JSON on success, plain text
on `404`).

## Walkthrough

### Full context plus MockMvc

```kotlin
@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration::class)
class InventoryControllerTest @Autowired constructor(
    private val mockMvc: MockMvc,
    private val jdbcClient: JdbcClient,
) {
```

**Spring: `@SpringBootTest` + `@AutoConfigureMockMvc`.** `@SpringBootTest` starts the full
application context (see [InventoryApplicationTests.kt](../InventoryApplicationTests.kt.md)).
`@AutoConfigureMockMvc` adds a `MockMvc` bean. `MockMvc` sends a fake HTTP request straight into
Spring MVC's `DispatcherServlet`, in the same JVM and on the same thread, with no real server or
network port. Everything after that is real: request mapping, the controller, Jackson and the
database.

**Why full stack rather than `@WebMvcTest`:** `@WebMvcTest` starts only the web layer and needs
the service replaced by a mock. For a read-only endpoint with no branching, the full path to a
real database is more convincing and needs no mocking library. When the error paths arrive
(`400`/`404`), a `@WebMvcTest` with a mocked service may become the better fit. For the `404` of
`GET /inventory/{skuId}` we stayed full stack: "missing" just means "no row", which is easy to set
up for real, and it checks the whole path from the empty query to the plain-text response.

**Kotlin:** `@Autowired constructor` is explained in
[InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md).

**Spring: context caching.** This class uses a different set of annotations from
`InventoryApplicationTests`, so Spring caches a separate context for it, with its own Postgres
container (see [TestcontainersConfiguration.kt](../support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md)).

### A clean table before every test

```kotlin
/** Starts every test from an empty table, since all tests in this context share one database. */
@BeforeEach
fun clearInventory() {
    jdbcClient.sql("DELETE FROM inventory").update()
}
```

**Spring / JUnit: `@BeforeEach`.** JUnit calls this before each `@Test` method.

**Why explicit cleanup instead of `@Transactional` rollback** (which `InventoryRepositoryTest`
uses): rollback only covers work done on the test's own thread. MockMvc happens to run on that
thread, but the concurrency tests in the oversell test plan will send requests from many
threads at once. Starting with explicit cleanup keeps all the web tests using the same pattern.
Cleaning up *before* each test instead of after means a test that crashes halfway can't break
the next one.

The `insert` helper is the same as in
[InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md).

### Empty inventory returns `[]`

```kotlin
/** Contract: "If no SKUs exist, returns an empty array." */
@Test
fun `GET inventory returns an empty JSON array when there are no SKUs`() {
    mockMvc.get("/inventory").andExpect {
        status { isOk() }
        content {
            contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            json("[]", JsonCompareMode.STRICT)
        }
    }
}
```

**Kotlin: extension functions.** `MockMvc` is a Java class with no `get` method. The import
`org.springframework.test.web.servlet.get` brings in an **extension function** that Spring ships
for Kotlin. It's declared outside the class as `fun MockMvc.get(...)`, but it's called as if it
were a member. Under the hood it's a static method that takes the `MockMvc` as its first
argument, so it can't reach private members. Java can't do this; you'd call a static helper
yourself.

**Kotlin: the MockMvc DSL.** `andExpect { ... }` takes a *lambda with receiver*: inside the braces,
`this` is a matcher builder, so `status { }` and `content { }` are its methods, called without
a prefix. That's the same mechanism as Gradle's `dependencies { }` (see
[build.gradle.kts](../../build.gradle.kts.md)). The Java version of the same test:

```java
mockMvc.perform(get("/inventory"))
       .andExpect(status().isOk())
       .andExpect(content().contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON))
       .andExpect(content().json("[]", JsonCompareMode.STRICT));
```

**Spring: `JsonCompareMode.STRICT`.** `json(...)` compares JSON structure, not text, so spaces
and property order inside an object don't matter. `STRICT` also fails on extra properties and
on array elements in a different order. The default, `LENIENT`, allows both, which would let an
unexpected field or an ordering bug slip through.

**Contract:** status `200`, content type `application/json`, body `[]`.

### Rows become JSON objects, in SKU order

```kotlin
@Test
fun `GET inventory returns every SKU with its quantity`() {
    insert("widget", 5)
    insert("CW-XYCS-BM-01", 10)
    insert("sold-out", 0)

    mockMvc.get("/inventory").andExpect {
        status { isOk() }
        content {
            contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            json(
                """
                [
                  {"skuId": "CW-XYCS-BM-01", "quantity": 10},
                  {"skuId": "sold-out", "quantity": 0},
                  {"skuId": "widget", "quantity": 5}
                ]
                """,
                JsonCompareMode.STRICT,
            )
        }
    }
}
```

**Kotlin: raw strings.** `"""..."""` is a raw string: quotes inside need no escaping and line
breaks are kept. It's like Java's text block `"""`, but Kotlin doesn't strip the indentation
unless you call `.trimIndent()`. Here the extra spaces don't matter, because JSON comparison
ignores whitespace.

**Why this one test covers so much:** `STRICT` checks the property names `skuId` and `quantity`
(so a renamed Kotlin property fails here), that values are numbers rather than strings, that no
extra fields appear, the order, and that a zero-stock SKU is included.

**Contract:** a JSON array of `InventoryItem` objects, `{"skuId": string, "quantity": integer}`.

**Renaming a property breaks exactly one test.** If `skuId` became `sku` in `InventoryItem`
(and everything still compiled), the repository tests would pass (they compare objects, and the
constructor takes arguments by position), and the empty-array test would pass (`[]` has no fields).
Only `GET inventory returns every SKU with its quantity` fails, because Jackson would write
`"sku"` and STRICT expects `"skuId"`. This test is what keeps the JSON in line with the contract.

### One SKU as a JSON object

```kotlin
/** Contract: 200 with a single InventoryItem as JSON. */
@Test
fun `GET inventory by SKU returns the item`() {
    insert("CW-XYCS-BM-01", 10)
    insert("widget", 5)

    mockMvc.get("/inventory/CW-XYCS-BM-01").andExpect {
        status { isOk() }
        content {
            contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            json("""{"skuId": "CW-XYCS-BM-01", "quantity": 10}""", JsonCompareMode.STRICT)
        }
    }
}
```

**Why the contract's example SKU:** `CW-XYCS-BM-01` is the example in inventory.yaml. Dashes
are ordinary URL path characters, so it reaches the controller unchanged as the `{skuId}` path
variable. The second row makes sure the endpoint returns the SKU that was asked for, not just
the only one in the table.

**Contract:** `200`, `application/json`, a single `InventoryItem` object (not an array).

### Zero stock is a 200

```kotlin
/** A sold-out SKU exists, so it is a 200 with quantity 0, not a 404. */
@Test
fun `GET inventory by SKU returns zero stock as 200`() {
    insert("sold-out", 0)

    mockMvc.get("/inventory/sold-out").andExpect {
        status { isOk() }
        content {
            contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            json("""{"skuId": "sold-out", "quantity": 0}""", JsonCompareMode.STRICT)
        }
    }
}
```

**Why:** the contract returns 404 only if the SKU "does not exist". A sold-out SKU exists. An
implementation that treated `quantity == 0` as missing would fail here.

### A missing SKU is a plain-text 404

```kotlin
// Why: contentTypeCompatibleWith ignores parameters, so "text/plain;charset=UTF-8" also passes.
/** Contract: 404 with a `text/plain` Error string, not JSON. Message text agreed with Robert. */
@Test
fun `GET inventory by SKU returns 404 text for a missing SKU`() {
    mockMvc.get("/inventory/missing").andExpect {
        status { isNotFound() }
        content {
            contentTypeCompatibleWith(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
            string("SKU not found: missing")
        }
    }
}
```

**Spring: `contentType` vs `contentTypeCompatibleWith`.** `contentType(X)` requires an exact
match, *including parameters*. A `text/plain` response can carry a character set,
`text/plain;charset=UTF-8`, and that is still `text/plain`. So the test uses
`contentTypeCompatibleWith`, which compares only the type and subtype. Today the app sends plain
`text/plain` with no charset (checked with `curl` on 2026-09-27): the handler sets the Content-Type
itself, and the message converter only adds its default charset when no Content-Type is set. The
looser check keeps the test passing if a `charset=UTF-8` is added later (a TODO item). The JSON tests keep the
exact `contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)`, because Spring doesn't add a charset there.

**Spring: `string(...)`.** It compares the whole body as text, exactly. `json(...)` would be
wrong here: the contract's `Error` schema is a bare string, not a JSON document.

**Contract:** `404`, `text/plain`, an `Error` string. The message `SKU not found: <skuId>` was
Robert's choice on 2026-09-27, because the contract gives no example for the 404.

**Why this is the test that shapes the error handling:** an exception that escapes a controller
with no handler becomes a `500`, and `ResponseStatusException` gives no `text/plain` body (in MockMvc
the body is empty; in the running app Boot renders a JSON or HTML error page). Only a
handler that sets the status, the content type and the body passes all three checks.

### Case-sensitive at the HTTP level too

```kotlin
/** SKU ids match case-sensitively, so a SKU that differs only in case is not found. */
@Test
fun `GET inventory by SKU is case-sensitive`() {
    insert("widget", 5)

    mockMvc.get("/inventory/WIDGET").andExpect {
        status { isNotFound() }
        content {
            contentTypeCompatibleWith(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
            string("SKU not found: WIDGET")
        }
    }
}
```

**Why repeat the repository's case test here:** the repository test proves the query is exact.
This one proves that nothing between HTTP and the query changes the SKU (lowercasing it in the
controller, say), and that the error message echoes the SKU exactly as it was requested.

- If `InventoryItem` gained a third property, `lastUpdated`, which assertion would fail, and
  would it still fail with `LENIENT`?
- Why is the cleanup a `DELETE` in `@BeforeEach` here, when the repository test needs none?
- Why does the `404` test use `contentTypeCompatibleWith` while the `200` tests use
  `contentType`?
- Which test fails if the service treats `quantity == 0` as "not found"? What status would it
  see?
- What would the `404` test report if the exception escaped with no handler at all?
### Case-sensitive match

```kotlin
// Why: SKU ids are an exact, case-sensitive match for now (README "Column types" decision).
/** `WIDGET` and `widget` are different SKUs. */
@Test
fun `findBySkuId matches the SKU id case-sensitively`() {
    insert("widget", 5)

    assertNull(inventoryRepository.findBySkuId("WIDGET"))
}
```

**Why:** Postgres compares `TEXT` case-sensitively, so a plain `WHERE sku_id = ?` already
behaves this way. The test pins the current decision. If we later choose to normalize case (an
open question for `POST`), this is the test that has to change, which makes that change a
visible decision rather than an accident.

### The database backstop

```kotlin
@Test
fun `database rejects an update that would make quantity negative`() {
    insert("widget", 1)

    assertFailsWith<DataIntegrityViolationException> {
        jdbcClient.sql("UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - 2 WHERE sku_id = ?")
            .param("widget")
            .update()
    }
}
```

**Why this bypasses the repository:** the point is to show what happens if application code
is wrong. The `UPDATE` deliberately has no `quantity >= ?` guard, so the only thing stopping it
is the `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint from
[V1__create_inventory.sql](../../main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md).

**Kotlin: `assertFailsWith<T> { ... }`.** It runs the lambda and passes only if the lambda throws
a `T`. It returns the exception if you want to inspect it. `T` is a reified type parameter (see
[InventoryApplication.kt](../../main/InventoryApplication.kt.md)), which is how the function can
check the exception type at runtime. JUnit's version is `assertThrows(X.class, () -> ...)`.

**Spring:** Postgres answers with SQLSTATE `23514` (check violation). Spring's exception
translation maps it to `DataIntegrityViolationException`, a database-independent exception, so
the test doesn't depend on Postgres error codes.

The failed statement aborts the test's transaction in Postgres, and the rollback at the end of
the test discards everything anyway.

## Role

Tests `GET /inventory` and `GET /inventory/{skuId}` through the whole stack: MockMvc →
controller → service → repository → real Postgres. It checks exactly what the contract
specifies: the status code, the `Content-Type` and the exact body (JSON on success, plain text
on `404`).

## Walkthrough

### Full context plus MockMvc

```kotlin
@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration::class)
class InventoryControllerTest @Autowired constructor(
    private val mockMvc: MockMvc,
    private val jdbcClient: JdbcClient,
) {
```

**Spring: `@SpringBootTest` + `@AutoConfigureMockMvc`.** `@SpringBootTest` starts the full
application context (see [InventoryApplicationTests.kt](../InventoryApplicationTests.kt.md)).
`@AutoConfigureMockMvc` adds a `MockMvc` bean. `MockMvc` sends a fake HTTP request straight into
Spring MVC's `DispatcherServlet`, in the same JVM and on the same thread, with no real server or
network port. Everything after that is real: request mapping, the controller, Jackson and the
database.

**Why full stack rather than `@WebMvcTest`:** `@WebMvcTest` starts only the web layer and needs
the service replaced by a mock. For a read-only endpoint with no branching, the full path to a
real database is more convincing and needs no mocking library. When the error paths arrive
(`400`/`404`), a `@WebMvcTest` with a mocked service may become the better fit. For the `404` of
`GET /inventory/{skuId}` we stayed full stack: "missing" just means "no row", which is easy to set
up for real, and it checks the whole path from the empty query to the plain-text response.

**Kotlin:** `@Autowired constructor` is explained in
[InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md).

**Spring: context caching.** This class uses a different set of annotations from
`InventoryApplicationTests`, so Spring caches a separate context for it, with its own Postgres
container (see [TestcontainersConfiguration.kt](../support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md)).

### A clean table before every test

```kotlin
/** Starts every test from an empty table, since all tests in this context share one database. */
@BeforeEach
fun clearInventory() {
    jdbcClient.sql("DELETE FROM inventory").update()
}
```

**Spring / JUnit: `@BeforeEach`.** JUnit calls this before each `@Test` method.

**Why explicit cleanup instead of `@Transactional` rollback** (which `InventoryRepositoryTest`
uses): rollback only covers work done on the test's own thread. MockMvc happens to run on that
thread, but the concurrency tests in the oversell test plan will send requests from many
threads at once. Starting with explicit cleanup keeps all the web tests using the same pattern.
Cleaning up *before* each test instead of after means a test that crashes halfway can't break
the next one.

The `insert` helper is the same as in
[InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md).

### Empty inventory returns `[]`

```kotlin
/** Contract: "If no SKUs exist, returns an empty array." */
@Test
fun `GET inventory returns an empty JSON array when there are no SKUs`() {
    mockMvc.get("/inventory").andExpect {
        status { isOk() }
        content {
            contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            json("[]", JsonCompareMode.STRICT)
        }
    }
}
```

`org.springframework.test.web.servlet.get` brings in an **extension function** that Spring ships
for Kotlin. It's declared outside the class as `fun MockMvc.get(...)`, but it's called as if it
were a member. Under the hood it's a static method that takes the `MockMvc` as its first
argument, so it can't reach private members. Java can't do this; you'd call a static helper
yourself.

a prefix. That's the same mechanism as Gradle's `dependencies { }` (see
[build.gradle.kts](../../build.gradle.kts.md)). The Java version of the same test:

```java
mockMvc.perform(get("/inventory"))

       .andExpect(content().contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON))
       .andExpect(content().json("[]", JsonCompareMode.STRICT));
```

and property order inside an object don't matter. `STRICT` also fails on extra properties and
on array elements in a different order. The default, `LENIENT`, allows both, which would let an
unexpected field or an ordering bug slip through.

```kotlin
    insert("widget", 5)

        status { isOk() }

            contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)

                  {"skuId": "widget", "quantity": 5}

    }

```

breaks are kept. It's like Java's text block `"""`, but Kotlin doesn't strip the indentation
unless you call `.trimIndent()`. Here the extra spaces don't matter, because JSON comparison
ignores whitespace.

  would it still fail with `LENIENT`?
- Why is the cleanup a `DELETE` in `@BeforeEach` here, when the repository test needs none?
- Why does the `404` test use `contentTypeCompatibleWith` while the `200` tests use
  `contentType`?
- Which test fails if the service treats `quantity == 0` as "not found"? What status would it
  see?
- What would the `404` test report if the exception escaped with no handler at all?
### Case-sensitive match

```kotlin
// Why: SKU ids are an exact, case-sensitive match for now (README "Column types" decision).
/** `WIDGET` and `widget` are different SKUs. */
@Test
fun `findBySkuId matches the SKU id case-sensitively`() {
    insert("widget", 5)

    assertNull(inventoryRepository.findBySkuId("WIDGET"))
}
```

**Why:** Postgres compares `TEXT` case-sensitively, so a plain `WHERE sku_id = ?` already
behaves this way. The test pins the current decision. If we later choose to normalize case (an
open question for `POST`), this is the test that has to change, which makes that change a
visible decision rather than an accident.

### The database backstop

```kotlin
@Test
fun `database rejects an update that would make quantity negative`() {
    insert("widget", 1)

    assertFailsWith<DataIntegrityViolationException> {
        jdbcClient.sql("UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - 2 WHERE sku_id = ?")
            .param("widget")
            .update()
    }
}
```

**Why this bypasses the repository:** the point is to show what happens if application code
is wrong. The `UPDATE` deliberately has no `quantity >= ?` guard, so the only thing stopping it
is the `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint from
[V1__create_inventory.sql](../../main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md).

**Kotlin: `assertFailsWith<T> { ... }`.** It runs the lambda and passes only if the lambda throws
a `T`. It returns the exception if you want to inspect it. `T` is a reified type parameter (see
[InventoryApplication.kt](../../main/InventoryApplication.kt.md)), which is how the function can
check the exception type at runtime. JUnit's version is `assertThrows(X.class, () -> ...)`.

**Spring:** Postgres answers with SQLSTATE `23514` (check violation). Spring's exception
translation maps it to `DataIntegrityViolationException`, a database-independent exception, so
the test doesn't depend on Postgres error codes.

The failed statement aborts the test's transaction in Postgres, and the rollback at the end of
the test discards everything anyway.


controller that echoes the request back. Reading the row proves the stock was stored.

**Contract:** the `post` operation lists only `200` for success. `201 Created` is the usual REST

### POST adds to an existing SKU

```kotlin
@Test
fun `POST inventory adds to an existing SKU`() {
    insert("widget", 5)

    postInventory("widget", """{"quantity": 3}""").andExpect {
        ...
            json("""{"skuId": "widget", "quantity": 8}""", JsonCompareMode.STRICT)
        ...
    }
    assertEquals(8, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**Contract:** "If it already exists, the quantity is added to the current stock. Returns the
updated inventory state." The body is the new total (8), not the amount posted (3).

```kotlin
/** Contract: `quantity` has `minimum: 1`, so 0 and negatives are a 400 and stock is untouched. */
@ParameterizedTest(name = "quantity {0}")
@ValueSource(ints = [0, -5])
fun `POST inventory rejects a quantity below 1`(quantity: Int) {
    insert("widget", 5)

    postInventory("widget", """{"quantity": $quantity}""")
        .andExpectBadRequest("quantity must be at least 1")
    assertEquals(5, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**JUnit: parameterized tests.** `@ParameterizedTest` runs the method once per value from the
source; `@ValueSource(ints = [0, -5])` supplies the values, and each one arrives as the
`quantity` parameter. `name = "quantity {0}"` sets the display name, so the report shows
`quantity 0` and `quantity -5` as separate results. The Java version is the same annotations with
`ints = {0, -5}`.

**Kotlin: array literals in annotations.** `[0, -5]` is Kotlin's syntax for an array argument
inside an annotation (Java uses `{0, -5}`). Outside annotations you'd write `intArrayOf(0, -5)`.

**Kotlin: a template inside a raw string.** `"""{"quantity": $quantity}"""` works because raw
strings still expand `$name` templates (see
[SkuNotFoundException.kt](../../main/inventory/error/SkuNotFoundException.kt.md)).

**Why `-5` as well as `0`:** `0` is the boundary. `-5` guards against a check written as
`quantity != 0`. Without the check, a negative "receive" would quietly remove stock.

**Contract:** `InventoryQuantity.quantity` has `minimum: 1`; `400` is `text/plain`. The message

```kotlin

    postInventory("new-sku", """{"quantity": 0}""")
        .andExpectBadRequest("quantity must be at least 1")
    assertNull(quantityOf("new-sku"))
}
```

**Why:** an implementation could insert the SKU first and only then fail on the quantity,
leaving a `new-sku` row with 0 stock behind. This test fails if validation doesn't happen

### Every unreadable body is a 400

```kotlin
/** Any body that isn't `{"quantity": <whole number that fits in Int>}` is a 400 text/plain. */
@ParameterizedTest(name = "body [{0}]")
@ValueSource(
    strings = [
        "",
        "{",
        "null",
        "[5]",
        "{}",
        """{"quantity": null}""",
        """{"quantity": "5"}""",
        """{"quantity": 1.5}""",
        """{"quantity": 3000000000}""",
    ],
)
fun `POST inventory rejects an unreadable body`(body: String) {
    insert("widget", 5)

    postInventory("widget", body).andExpectBadRequest("Invalid request body")
    assertEquals(5, quantityOf("widget"))
```

Each body fails a different way:

| Body | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- |
| `""` | no body at all; the contract says `required: true` |
| `{` | not valid JSON |
| `null` | valid JSON, but no object; a required `@RequestBody` can't be `null` |
| `[5]` | an array, not an object |
| `{}` | `quantity` is missing; the contract says `required: [quantity]` |
| `{"quantity": null}` | `quantity` is a non-null `Int` in Kotlin |
| `{"quantity": "5"}` | a string, not an integer; lenient Jackson would coerce it |
| `{"quantity": 1.5}` | not a whole number; lenient Jackson would truncate it to 1 |
| `{"quantity": 3000000000}` | a whole number, but too big for `Int` |

**Spring:** all of these fail while Spring is still turning the body into the controller's
parameter, before the controller runs. Spring reports them as one exception type,
`HttpMessageNotReadableException`, which is why they share one message.

**Why `"5"` and `1.5` matter most:** they are the rows that fail only because we chose strict
mode. With Jackson's lenient defaults, `1.5` would quietly receive 1 unit, and nobody would
notice. That is the argument for the "strict" decision in the README.

**Why `3000000000`:** it is bigger than `Int.MAX_VALUE` (2,147,483,647), so it can't be read into
an `Int`. That's different from the overflow test below, where each number fits but their sum
doesn't.

```kotlin
@Test
fun `POST inventory rejects a non-JSON content type`() {
    insert("widget", 5)

    postInventory("widget", "5", MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
        .andExpectBadRequest("Content-Type must be application/json")
    assertEquals(5, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**Spring:** `@RequestBody` looks for a message converter that can read the request's
`Content-Type` into `InventoryQuantity`. Only the JSON converter can, so a `text/plain` request
fails with `HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException`. By default Spring answers that with
`415 Unsupported Media Type`, which is correct HTTP, but the contract lists only `400`.

### Overflow is a 400 and changes nothing

```kotlin
/** Stock is an Int; a total past Int.MAX_VALUE is an invalid request (400), not a 500, and nothing changes. */
@Test
fun `POST inventory rejects an add that would overflow the stock`() {
    insert("widget", Int.MAX_VALUE - 1)

    postInventory("widget", """{"quantity": 2}""")
        .andExpectBadRequest("Quantity would exceed the maximum stock")
    assertEquals(Int.MAX_VALUE - 1, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**Why:** both numbers are valid on their own; only the sum is too big. The repository catches
this in its SQL (see [InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md)); this test
checks that the "no row came back" answer turns into a plain-text `400` rather than a `500`.


[InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md).

### Helpers for POST

```kotlin
private fun postInventory(
    skuId: String,
    body: String,
    mediaType: MediaType = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON,
): ResultActionsDsl =
    mockMvc.post("/inventory/$skuId") {
        contentType = mediaType
        content = body
    }

private fun ResultActionsDsl.andExpectBadRequest(message: String) = andExpect {
    status { isBadRequest() }
    content {
        contentTypeCompatibleWith(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
        string(message)
    }
}
```

**Kotlin: default arguments.** `mediaType: MediaType = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON` gives the
parameter a default, so most calls are `postInventory("widget", body)` and only the content-type
test passes a third argument. Java has no default arguments; you'd write an overload
`postInventory(skuId, body)` that calls the three-argument one.

**Kotlin: the request-building lambda.** `mockMvc.post(url) { ... }` is another extension
function, like `get`. Its lambda has a request builder as its receiver, so `contentType = ...`
and `content = ...` set that builder's properties. The body is sent exactly as written. Nothing
parses it on the way out, which is how the tests can send broken JSON.

**Kotlin: writing your own extension function.** `ResultActionsDsl.andExpectBadRequest` is
declared here, in the test class, and it's `private`, so it exists only inside this class. It lets
every `400` test say `postInventory(...).andExpectBadRequest("...")` in one line. Inside it,
`andExpect { ... }` is called on `this`, the `ResultActionsDsl` it was called on. The return type
is inferred from `andExpect`, which returns the same `ResultActionsDsl`, so calls can chain.

### POST creates a new SKU

```kotlin
/** Contract: a new SKU "is created with the given quantity"; 200 (not 201) with the InventoryItem as JSON. */
@Test
fun `POST inventory creates a new SKU`() {
    postInventory("CW-XYCS-BM-01", """{"quantity": 10}""").andExpect {
        status { isOk() }
        content {
            contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            json("""{"skuId": "CW-XYCS-BM-01", "quantity": 10}""", JsonCompareMode.STRICT)
        }
    }
    assertEquals(10, quantityOf("CW-XYCS-BM-01"))
}
```

**Why check the table as well as the response:** a controller that echoed the request back
could fake the response. Reading the row proves the stock was stored.

**Contract:** the `post` operation lists only `200` for success. `201 Created` is the usual REST
answer for "created", but a `201` would break the contract, so the test pins `isOk()`.

### POST adds to an existing SKU

```kotlin
@Test
fun `POST inventory adds to an existing SKU`() {
    insert("widget", 5)

    postInventory("widget", """{"quantity": 3}""").andExpect {
        ...
            json("""{"skuId": "widget", "quantity": 8}""", JsonCompareMode.STRICT)
        ...
    }
    assertEquals(8, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**Contract:** "If it already exists, the quantity is added to the current stock. Returns the
updated inventory state." The body holds the new total (8), not the amount posted (3).

### Quantities below 1

```kotlin
/** Contract: `quantity` has `minimum: 1`, so 0 and negatives are a 400 and stock is untouched. */
@ParameterizedTest(name = "quantity {0}")
@ValueSource(ints = [0, -5])
fun `POST inventory rejects a quantity below 1`(quantity: Int) {
    insert("widget", 5)

    postInventory("widget", """{"quantity": $quantity}""")
        .andExpectBadRequest("quantity must be at least 1")
    assertEquals(5, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**JUnit: parameterized tests.** `@ParameterizedTest` runs the method once for each value from
the source. `@ValueSource(ints = [0, -5])` supplies the values, and each one arrives as the
`quantity` parameter. `name = "quantity {0}"` sets the display name, so the report lists
`quantity 0` and `quantity -5` as separate results.

**Kotlin: array literals in annotations.** `[0, -5]` is Kotlin's syntax for an array argument
inside an annotation. Java writes it `{0, -5}`. Outside annotations you'd write `intArrayOf(0, -5)`.

**Kotlin: a template inside a raw string.** `"""{"quantity": $quantity}"""` works because raw
strings still expand `$name` templates (see
[SkuNotFoundException.kt](../../main/inventory/error/SkuNotFoundException.kt.md)).

**Why `-5` as well as `0`:** `0` is the boundary. `-5` catches a check written as
`quantity != 0`. Without it, a negative "receive" would quietly remove stock.

**Contract:** `InventoryQuantity.quantity` has `minimum: 1`, and the `400` is `text/plain`. The
message was agreed with Robert on 2026-09-28.

### A rejected POST creates nothing

```kotlin
@Test
fun `POST inventory with an invalid quantity does not create the SKU`() {
    postInventory("new-sku", """{"quantity": 0}""")
        .andExpectBadRequest("quantity must be at least 1")
    assertNull(quantityOf("new-sku"))
}
```

**Why:** an implementation could insert the SKU first and only then fail on the quantity,
leaving a `new-sku` row with 0 stock behind. This test fails unless validation happens
before anything is written.

### Every unreadable body is a 400

```kotlin
// Why: strict JSON (README "Contract gaps" decision, 2026-09-28). Jackson's defaults would turn
// "5" into 5 and 1.5 into 1; stock counts must never be guessed.
/** Any body that isn't `{"quantity": <whole number that fits in Int>}` is a 400 text/plain. */
@ParameterizedTest(name = "body [{0}]")
@ValueSource(
    strings = [
        "",
        "{",
        "null",
        "[5]",
        "{}",
        """{"quantity": null}""",
        """{"quantity": "5"}""",
        """{"quantity": 1.5}""",
        """{"quantity": 3000000000}""",
    ],
)
fun `POST inventory rejects an unreadable body`(body: String) {
    insert("widget", 5)

    postInventory("widget", body).andExpectBadRequest("Invalid request body")
    assertEquals(5, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

Each body fails in a different way:

| Body | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- |
| `""` | no body at all; the contract says `required: true` |
| `{` | not valid JSON |
| `null` | valid JSON, but not an object; a required `@RequestBody` can't be `null` |
| `[5]` | an array, not an object |
| `{}` | `quantity` is missing; the contract says `required: [quantity]` |
| `{"quantity": null}` | `quantity` is a non-null `Int` in Kotlin |
| `{"quantity": "5"}` | a string, not an integer; lenient Jackson would coerce it |
| `{"quantity": 1.5}` | not a whole number; lenient Jackson would truncate it to 1 |
| `{"quantity": 3000000000}` | a whole number, but too big for an `Int` |

**Spring:** each of these fails while Spring is still turning the body into the controller's
parameter, before the controller runs. Spring reports them all as one exception type,
`HttpMessageNotReadableException`, which is why they share one message.

**Why `"5"` and `1.5` matter most:** these two rows fail only because we chose strict mode.
With Jackson's lenient defaults, `1.5` would quietly receive 1 unit, and nobody would
notice. That's the argument for the "strict" decision in the README.

**Why `3000000000`:** it's bigger than `Int.MAX_VALUE` (2,147,483,647), so it can't be read into
an `Int`. The overflow test below is different: there each number fits, but their sum
doesn't.

### Wrong content type is a 400, not a 415

```kotlin
// Why: Spring's default is 415, which the contract doesn't list (README "Contract gaps" decision, 2026-09-28).
/** The contract only accepts `application/json`; anything else is a 400 text/plain. */
@Test
fun `POST inventory rejects a non-JSON content type`() {
    insert("widget", 5)

    postInventory("widget", "5", MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
        .andExpectBadRequest("Content-Type must be application/json")
    assertEquals(5, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**Spring:** `@RequestBody` looks for a message converter that can read the request's
`Content-Type` into `InventoryQuantity`. Only the JSON converter can, so a `text/plain` request
fails with `HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException`. Spring's default answer is
`415 Unsupported Media Type`. That's correct HTTP, but the contract lists only `400`.

### Overflow is a 400 and changes nothing

```kotlin
/** Stock is an Int; a total past Int.MAX_VALUE is an invalid request (400), not a 500, and nothing changes. */
@Test
fun `POST inventory rejects an add that would overflow the stock`() {
    insert("widget", Int.MAX_VALUE - 1)

    postInventory("widget", """{"quantity": 2}""")
        .andExpectBadRequest("Quantity would exceed the maximum stock")
    assertEquals(Int.MAX_VALUE - 1, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**Why:** both numbers are valid on their own; only the sum is too big. The repository catches
this in its SQL (see [InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md)). This test
checks that the repository's "no row came back" answer becomes a plain-text `400`, not a `500`.

### Case-sensitive POST

```kotlin
/** SKU ids match case-sensitively, so posting to `WIDGET` creates a separate SKU. */
@Test
fun `POST inventory is case-sensitive`() {
    insert("widget", 5)

    postInventory("WIDGET", """{"quantity": 2}""").andExpect {
        status { isOk() }
        content { json("""{"skuId": "WIDGET", "quantity": 2}""", JsonCompareMode.STRICT) }
    }
    assertEquals(5, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**Why:** this is the "exact match" decision (README, 2026-09-28) checked over HTTP. `WIDGET`
becomes its own SKU, and `widget` keeps its 5.

# InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt

> Source: [src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt](../../../../../src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-28

## Role

This is the first part of the **concurrency** section of the oversell test plan in
[TODO.md](../../../../../.claude/TODO.md). Many threads call `InventoryRepository.addStock` for the
same SKU at the same moment, and the tests check that no update is lost and none fails. The
purchase race tests will join this class when `POST /inventory/{skuId}/purchase` exists.

The other test classes send one request at a time, so they can't catch a race. This one can.

## Walkthrough

### Why a full context and not `@JdbcTest`

```kotlin
// Why: @SpringBootTest, not @JdbcTest. @JdbcTest wraps each test in a rolled-back transaction on one
// connection, so rows written by the worker threads' own connections would never be visible to it.
/**
 * Oversell test plan, concurrency section: ...
 */
@SpringBootTest
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration::class)
class InventoryConcurrencyTest @Autowired constructor(
    private val inventoryRepository: InventoryRepository,
    private val jdbcClient: JdbcClient,
) {
```

**Spring: test transactions are per thread.** `@JdbcTest` (see
[InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md)) opens a transaction on the test's
thread and rolls it back at the end. Spring ties that transaction to the **thread**. Worker
threads started by the test aren't part of it: each takes its own connection from the pool and
commits on its own. That causes two problems:

- The test's `SELECT` runs inside its transaction and can't see the threads' committed rows the
  way we want, and any row the test inserted before the race is uncommitted and invisible to
  the threads.
- The workers' rows are committed for real, so the rollback wouldn't clean them up.

So this class runs with no test transaction. Every call commits, exactly like in production,
and the `@BeforeEach` `DELETE` does the cleanup (the same pattern as
[InventoryControllerTest.kt](InventoryControllerTest.kt.md)).

**Spring: context caching.** These annotations differ from `InventoryControllerTest` (there's no
`@AutoConfigureMockMvc`), so Spring caches a separate context for this class, with its own
Postgres container. That costs a few seconds of startup, and in return the class doesn't depend on
MockMvc, which isn't meant to be called from many threads.

### The start gate

```kotlin
// Why: a start gate. Every thread first checks in on `ready`, then waits on `start`; releasing
// `start` once makes them all hit the database together instead of one after another.
private fun <T> race(threads: Int, action: (Int) -> T): List<Result<T>> {
    val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads)
    val ready = CountDownLatch(threads)
    val start = CountDownLatch(1)
    try {
        val futures = (0 until threads).map { i ->
            pool.submit(Callable {
                ready.countDown()
                start.await()
                action(i)
            })
        }
        ready.await()
        start.countDown()
        return futures.map { runCatching { it.get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) } }
    } finally {
        pool.shutdownNow()
    }
}
```

**Why a gate at all:** starting 50 threads one by one in a loop spreads them out in time. The
first threads may finish before the last ones start, and then there's no race to test. The gate
makes them all wait at the same line and releases them together.

**Java concurrency: `CountDownLatch`.** A counter threads can wait on. `countDown()` decrements
it; `await()` blocks until it reaches zero. There are two latches here:

1. `ready` starts at `threads`. Each worker counts it down as it arrives, and the test thread's
   `ready.await()` returns once all of them are waiting.
2. `start` starts at 1. Every worker blocks on `start.await()`. The test's single
   `start.countDown()` releases all of them at once.

**Java concurrency: thread pool and futures.** `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads)` makes one
thread per worker, so all of them can wait at the gate together (a smaller pool would deadlock:
the queued tasks could never arrive at `ready`). `submit` returns a `Future`; `get(30, SECONDS)`
waits for its result and rethrows anything the task threw, wrapped in an `ExecutionException`.
The timeout makes a hung test fail instead of running forever. `shutdownNow()` in `finally`
stops the threads even when something failed.

**Kotlin: a generic function.** `fun <T> race(..., action: (Int) -> T): List<Result<T>>` works for
any result type. `T` is whatever `action` returns: `InventoryItem?` for `addStock`, and later
something else for purchases. Java writes it the same way: `<T> List<Result<T>> race(...)`.

**Kotlin: function types.** `action: (Int) -> T` is a parameter that holds a function taking an
`Int` (the thread's index) and returning a `T`. Java would use `IntFunction<T>` or
`Function<Integer, T>`. The call sites pass a trailing lambda: `race(threads) { i -> ... }`.

**Kotlin: `Callable { ... }`.** `submit` is overloaded for `Runnable` (no result) and `Callable`
(returns a result). Writing `Callable { ... }` picks the one that returns a value. This is a SAM
conversion, like the row mapper in [InventoryRepository.kt](../../main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md).

**Kotlin: ranges.** `0 until threads` is `0, 1, ..., threads - 1` (the end is excluded), and
`.map { i -> ... }` turns each index into a submitted task. Java: `IntStream.range(0, threads)`.

**Kotlin: `runCatching` and `Result`.** `runCatching { block }` runs the block and returns a
`Result`: a success holding the value, or a failure holding the exception. Nothing is thrown.
That lets the test collect *every* thread's outcome first, then assert on all of them together.
`exceptionOrNull()` and `getOrNull()` read the two sides. Java has no built-in equivalent; you'd
catch the exception in a loop and keep it in a list.

### The new-SKU creation race

```kotlin
@RepeatedTest(5)
fun `concurrent first-time adds for a new SKU all succeed and sum up`() {
    val threads = 50

    val results = race(threads) { i -> inventoryRepository.addStock("new-sku", i + 1) }

    val failures = results.mapNotNull { it.exceptionOrNull() }
    assertTrue(failures.isEmpty(), "adds failed: $failures")
    assertTrue(results.all { it.getOrNull() != null }, "an add returned null (treated as overflow)")
    assertEquals((1..threads).sum(), quantityOf("new-sku"))
}
```

**What it catches:** the naive way to "create or add" takes two steps. First check whether the
row exists, then either `INSERT` or `UPDATE`. Two threads can both see "no row" and both
`INSERT`. The second one fails with a duplicate-key error (the primary key), and its stock is
lost. A single `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` statement can't split like that: Postgres
handles the conflict inside the one statement.

**Why each thread adds a different amount (`i + 1`):** if every thread added the same amount,
losing one add and double-counting another would cancel out. With 1, 2, ..., 50 the expected
total is `(1..50).sum()` = 1275, and a lost or repeated add shows up in the final number.

**Kotlin: `mapNotNull`, `all`, `sum`.** `mapNotNull` maps each element and drops the `null`s,
leaving only the exceptions. `all { }` is `true` if the condition holds for every element.
`(1..threads).sum()` adds up an inclusive range (`..` includes the end, `until` doesn't).

**Kotlin: assertion messages.** The last argument of `assertTrue` is the message printed on
failure. `"adds failed: $failures"` shows *which* exceptions happened, which beats a bare
"expected true".

**JUnit: `@RepeatedTest(5)`.** Runs the test five times, each a separate result with its own
`@BeforeEach`. Races are intermittent; a broken implementation might pass once by luck, but
rarely five times in a row.

### The lost-update race

```kotlin
@RepeatedTest(5)
fun `concurrent adds to an existing SKU are never lost`() {
    jdbcClient.sql("INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES ('widget', 10)").update()
    val threads = 50

    val results = race(threads) { inventoryRepository.addStock("widget", 2) }

    val failures = results.mapNotNull { it.exceptionOrNull() }
    assertTrue(failures.isEmpty(), "adds failed: $failures")
    assertEquals(10 + threads * 2, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**What it catches:** a read-then-write implementation (read 10, compute 12, write 12). Two
threads that both read 10 both write 12, and one add disappears. That's a *lost update*. With
`SET quantity = inventory.quantity + EXCLUDED.quantity`, Postgres does the read and the write
under a row lock inside one statement, so the second thread waits and then adds to 12.

**Kotlin: an implicit lambda parameter.** `race(threads) { inventoryRepository.addStock(...) }`
doesn't use the index, so the lambda declares no parameter. A lambda with one parameter can
leave it out; if needed, it's available as `it`.

## Check your understanding

- Why would these tests be unreliable under `@JdbcTest`? Give both reasons.
- What happens to the race if you delete the `start` latch and keep only `ready`? And if you
  delete both?
- Why must the thread pool have `threads` threads, and not, say, 10?
- The new-SKU test adds `i + 1` rather than a constant. Describe a bug the constant version
  would miss.
- `race` returns `List<Result<T>>` instead of throwing on the first failure. What would the
  test report lose if it threw?
- Why run each test five times? Does passing five times prove there's no race?

+// Why: @SpringBootTest, not @JdbcTest. @JdbcTest's rolled-back transaction belongs to the test thread

+@SpringBootTest
+@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration::class)

+    private val inventoryRepository: InventoryRepository,
+    private val jdbcClient: JdbcClient,

+[InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md)) opens a transaction on the test's
+thread and rolls it back at the end. Spring ties that transaction to the **thread**. Worker
+threads started by the test aren't part of it: each takes its own connection from the pool and
+commits on its own. That causes two problems:
+- A row the test inserts before the race (`widget` with 10) is uncommitted, so the workers can't
+  see it. Worse, each worker's upsert would wait on that row's lock, which the test thread holds
+  until the rollback, so the race would hang until the timeout.
+- The workers' rows are committed for real, so the rollback wouldn't clean them up, and they'd
+  leak into the next test.
+So this class runs with no test transaction. Every call commits, exactly like in production,
+and the `@BeforeEach` `DELETE` does the cleanup (the same pattern as
+[InventoryControllerTest.kt](InventoryControllerTest.kt.md)).

+`@AutoConfigureMockMvc`), so Spring caches a separate context for this class, with its own
+Postgres container. That costs a few seconds of startup, and in return the class doesn't depend on
+MockMvc, which isn't meant to be called from many threads.

+```kotlin
+// Why: a start gate. Every thread first checks in on `ready`, then waits on `start`; releasing
+// `start` once makes them all hit the database together instead of one after another.
+private fun <T> race(threads: Int, action: (Int) -> T): List<Result<T>> {
+    val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads)
+    val ready = CountDownLatch(threads)
+    val start = CountDownLatch(1)
+    try {
+        val futures = (0 until threads).map { i ->
+            pool.submit(Callable {
+                ready.countDown()
+                start.await()
+                action(i)
+        ready.await()
+        start.countDown()
+        return futures.map { runCatching { it.get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) } }
+    } finally {
+        pool.shutdownNow()
+**Why a gate at all:** starting 50 threads one by one in a loop spreads them out in time. The
+first threads may finish before the last ones start, and then there's no race to test. The gate
+makes them all wait at the same line and releases them together.
+**Java concurrency: `CountDownLatch`.** A counter threads can wait on. `countDown()` decrements
+it; `await()` blocks until it reaches zero. There are two latches here:
+1. `ready` starts at `threads`. Each worker counts it down as it arrives, and the test thread's
+   `ready.await()` returns once all of them are waiting.
+2. `start` starts at 1. Every worker blocks on `start.await()`. The test's single
+   `start.countDown()` releases all of them at once.

+thread per worker, so all of them can wait at the gate together (a smaller pool would deadlock:
+the queued tasks could never arrive at `ready`). `submit` returns a `Future`; `get(30, SECONDS)`
+waits for its result and rethrows anything the task threw, wrapped in an `ExecutionException`.
+The timeout makes a hung test fail instead of running forever. `shutdownNow()` in `finally`
+stops the threads even when something failed.

+any result type. `T` is whatever `action` returns: `InventoryItem?` for `addStock`, and later
+something else for purchases. Java writes it the same way: `<T> List<Result<T>> race(...)`.
+**Kotlin: function types.** `action: (Int) -> T` is a parameter that holds a function taking an
+`Int` (the thread's index) and returning a `T`. Java would use `IntFunction<T>` or
+`Function<Integer, T>`. The call sites pass a trailing lambda: `race(threads) { i -> ... }`.
+**Kotlin: `Callable { ... }`.** `submit` is overloaded for `Runnable` (no result) and `Callable`
+(returns a result). Writing `Callable { ... }` picks the one that returns a value. This is a SAM
+conversion, like the row mapper in [InventoryRepository.kt](../../main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md).
+**Kotlin: ranges.** `0 until threads` is `0, 1, ..., threads - 1` (the end is excluded), and
+`.map { i -> ... }` turns each index into a submitted task. Java: `IntStream.range(0, threads)`.
+**Kotlin: `runCatching` and `Result`.** `runCatching { block }` runs the block and returns a
+`Result`: a success holding the value, or a failure holding the exception. Nothing is thrown.
+That lets the test collect *every* thread's outcome first, then assert on all of them together.
+`exceptionOrNull()` and `getOrNull()` read the two sides. Java has no built-in equivalent; you'd
+catch the exception in a loop and keep it in a list.

+```kotlin

+fun `concurrent first-time adds for a new SKU all succeed and sum up`() {
+    val threads = 50

75:| `@RequestMapping` + `@GetMapping` | Class-level base path plus method-level mappings; the function name doesn't matter | [InventoryController.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryController.kt.md) |
76:| Message converters (Jackson) | A `@ResponseBody` value is written as JSON; Kotlin property names become JSON keys | [InventoryController.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryController.kt.md) |
77:| The service layer | Business rules and error mapping sit between HTTP (controller) and SQL (repository) | [InventoryService.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md) |
78:| Singleton beans and threads | One bean instance, built at startup, serves every request thread at once, so beans must be stateless | [InventoryController.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryController.kt.md) |
79:| Named parameters in SQL | `:skuId` + `.param("skuId", value)` binds the value separately, preventing SQL injection | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md) |
80:| `@PathVariable` and path templates | `@GetMapping("/{skuId}")` matches one path segment and binds it to the same-named parameter | [InventoryController.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryController.kt.md) |
81:| Domain exceptions | The service throws a domain error (`SkuNotFoundException`); a handler decides the HTTP status | [SkuNotFoundException.kt](notes/main/inventory/error/SkuNotFoundException.kt.md) |
82:| `@RestControllerAdvice` + `@ExceptionHandler` | One class that catches exceptions from every controller; within a class the closest exception type wins, across advice classes their `@Order` decides first | [InventoryExceptionHandler.kt](notes/main/inventory/error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md) |
83:| Exception resolver chain | Spring catches every controller exception: `@ExceptionHandler` (controller, then advice) → `@ResponseStatus` → built-in mappings → `500` | [InventoryExceptionHandler.kt](notes/main/inventory/error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md) |
84:| When mistakes surface | Compile time (types), startup (missing beans), first request (strings: paths, SQL, missing advice); only request-level tests catch the last | [InventoryController.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryController.kt.md) |
85:| `ResponseEntity` builder | `status(...).contentType(...).body(...)` sets status, headers and body; `notFound()` has no body | [InventoryExceptionHandler.kt](notes/main/inventory/error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md) |
87:## Database and API design
89:| Concept | What it is | First seen |
90:| --- | --- | --- |
91:| Contract schemas are not tables | OpenAPI schemas describe JSON on the wire; tables describe what's stored | [V1__create_inventory.sql](notes/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md) |
92:| Natural vs surrogate key | `sku_id` as the primary key vs a generated `id` plus a unique `sku_id` | [V1__create_inventory.sql](notes/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md) |
93:| Constraints as a backstop | `PRIMARY KEY`, `NOT NULL`, `CHECK` protect data even when app code is wrong | [V1__create_inventory.sql](notes/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md) |
94:| Identifier case folding | Postgres lowercases unquoted names; use `snake_case` in SQL, `camelCase` in Kotlin | [V1__create_inventory.sql](notes/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md) |

-## Oversell protection: test plan
-**Invariant: a purchase must never oversell, even when requests arrive at the same moment.**
-Stock never goes below zero, and every unit sold was actually in stock. Test this at every
-level we build, using several different mechanisms, because each one catches a different
-class of bug. Each item below is also a teaching topic for a walkthrough.
-### Correctness in isolation
-- [ ] Repository tests against a real Postgres (Testcontainers, not H2): purchase exact stock → 0,
-      purchase stock + 1 → rejected and quantity unchanged, purchase on missing SKU → not found
-- [ ] Controller tests (`MockMvc`): 400 with `text/plain` body on insufficient stock, 404 on missing SKU
-### Concurrency
-- [ ] **Same-SKU purchase race.** Seed stock S, fire N > S concurrent purchases of 1 through
-      a start gate (`CountDownLatch` or coroutines) so they really overlap. Assert: exactly S
-      succeed (200), N − S are rejected (400), final quantity is 0, never negative.
-- [ ] **Uneven quantities.** Concurrent purchases of different sizes. Assert: the sum of
-      successful purchases ≤ S, and final = S − sum(successful).
-- [ ] **Mixed receive + purchase race.** Concurrent restocks and purchases. Assert:
-      final = initial + sum(received) − sum(successful purchases).
-- [ ] **New-SKU creation race.** Concurrent first-time `POST`s for a SKU that doesn't exist yet.
-      All succeed, no duplicate-key errors, final = sum of all quantities.
-- [ ] **Repeat to flush out flakiness.** Run the race tests many times (`@RepeatedTest`), since
-      concurrency bugs are intermittent.
-- [ ] **Negative control.** Temporarily swap in a naive read-then-write implementation and show
-      the race test *fails*. This proves the test can actually detect an oversell.
-### Database backstop
-- [ ] Test that the `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint rejects a direct update that would go
-      negative, so the database protects the data even if the application has a bug.
-      (test written in `InventoryRepositoryTest` 2026-09-24; passes once Robert's V1 migration exists)
-### Across instances and under load
-- [ ] **Multiple app instances.** Two app instances (or two Spring contexts) against the same
-      Postgres, running the purchase race. Correctness must hold because the database enforces it.
-- [ ] **HTTP load test.** Gatling (it has a Kotlin DSL) or k6 against the running app: sustained
-      concurrent purchases on hot SKUs, then check the final quantities with `GET /inventory`.
-### Model-based (stretch)
-- [ ] Property-based test (e.g. Kotest property testing): random sequences of receive and
-      purchase operations checked against a simple in-memory model. The invariant must hold
-      after every sequence.

-A running index of every Kotlin and Spring concept used in this codebase. Each row links to
